subject: biology

items.q: Why do phospholipids form a bilayer when they are mixed with water?
items.correct: Hydrophilic heads face the water and hydrophobic tails are shielded from it, so the sheet forms spontaneously.
items.misconception: The whole molecule repels water, so the phospholipids gather away from it as a droplet of oil.
items.why: Students learn that lipids are insoluble in water and picture fats and oils separating from water. They carry this over to phospholipids without noticing that the phosphate head makes one end of the molecule hydrophilic. Phospholipids are amphipathic: the phosphate head is hydrophilic and the two fatty acid tails are hydrophobic. In water they form a bilayer precisely because the heads can stay in contact with water while the tails are shielded from it.
items.specStatementText: Phospholipids form a bilayer by themselves
items.random_wrong: Enzymes in the cell join the phospholipids together into a sheet, using energy released from ATP.

items.q: A lipid is found to form a continuous sheet-like bilayer when shaken with water. Which property must the lipid have?
items.correct: It must be amphipathic, with a hydrophilic region and a hydrophobic region in each molecule.
items.misconception: It must be able to form covalent bonds with neighbouring lipid molecules in the sheet.
items.why: The other large biological structures studied in Theme B, such as polysaccharides and polypeptides, are polymers held together by covalent bonds, so students expect a membrane to be a covalent polymer too. Diagrams that draw the bilayer as a neat, solid-looking sheet reinforce this. Each phospholipid is a separate molecule. The bilayer is held together only by weak interactions, which is why phospholipids can move past one another, why the membrane is fluid, and why membranes can pinch off and fuse to form vesicles.
items.specStatementText: Phospholipids form a bilayer by themselves
items.random_wrong: It must be entirely hydrophobic, so that all of its molecules cluster together away from water.

items.q: Which of these particles crosses a pure phospholipid bilayer, with no proteins present, least readily?
items.correct: A sodium ion, which is small but charged and hydrophilic
items.misconception: A carbon dioxide molecule, which is larger than a water molecule
items.why: Earlier courses teach that 'small molecules can diffuse through the membrane' without saying which small molecules, and practicals with dialysis (Visking) tubing show a barrier that separates purely by size. The hydrophobic hydrocarbon chains at the core of a membrane have low permeability to large molecules and to hydrophilic particles, including ions and polar molecules. Permeability depends on both size and whether a particle is hydrophobic or hydrophilic, so a small ion is far less able to cross than a larger non-polar molecule.
items.random_wrong: An oxygen molecule, which needs a protein to cross the bilayer

items.q: A cell is respiring rapidly, so its internal oxygen concentration is low. How do oxygen molecules enter the cell?
items.correct: They pass between the phospholipids by simple diffusion down their gradient
items.misconception: They diffuse through a channel protein that is specific for oxygen and opens when needed
items.why: The word 'barrier' and the fact that nearly every membrane-transport diagram shows a protein lead students to conclude that the lipid part is impassable. Facilitated diffusion and active transport get more attention than simple diffusion. The bilayer is an effective barrier to ions, polar molecules and large molecules, but not to small non-polar molecules. Oxygen and carbon dioxide cross by simple diffusion between the phospholipids without any protein.
items.specStatementText: Simple diffusion: no protein, no energy
items.random_wrong: They are moved in by a pump protein using ATP, because the cell needs oxygen urgently

items.q: Which statement about membrane proteins is correct?
items.correct: Integral proteins are embedded in one or both lipid layers, while peripheral proteins are attached to a surface.
items.misconception: Integral and peripheral proteins are both transport proteins, differing only in the substance they carry.
items.why: The membrane proteins studied in most detail in this topic are those involved in diffusion and active transport, so students form the impression that transport is the only role of proteins in membranes. Membrane proteins are diverse in structure, location and function. Integral and peripheral proteins act as enzymes, hormone and neurotransmitter receptors, adhesion molecules and recognition molecules as well as transporters.
items.random_wrong: Integral proteins all span the whole bilayer, while peripheral proteins are embedded in only one layer.

items.q: An animal cell with a cytoplasmic solute concentration of 0.30 mol dm⁻³ is placed in a solution with a solute concentration of 0.10 mol dm⁻³. The membrane is impermeable to the solute. What happens?
items.correct: Net water movement is into the cell, because more free water molecules hit the membrane from the outside.
items.misconception: Water leaves the cell by osmosis, because water moves from the higher to the lower solute concentration.
items.why: Students apply the rule 'from high concentration to low concentration' to the concentration of the solute, which is the number given in the question, instead of to the concentration of water. In osmosis the net movement of water is from the solution with the lower solute concentration to the solution with the higher solute concentration. A lower solute concentration means a higher proportion of free water molecules, so more water molecules cross from that side.
items.random_wrong: Solute diffuses out of the cell until both sides reach 0.20 mol dm⁻³, and water then follows the solute out.

items.q: Some cells lining the kidney tubules have large numbers of aquaporins in their plasma membranes. What is the effect of these aquaporins?
items.correct: They greatly increase the rate at which water can cross the membrane by osmosis.
items.misconception: They pump water across the membrane against its gradient, using ATP energy.
items.why: Students associate proteins with 'doing work', and the everyday sense of 'facilitated' or 'carrier' suggests the protein is actively moving the substance. Active transport is often taught immediately after facilitated diffusion, and the two blur. Facilitated diffusion is passive: particles diffuse through a channel or carrier protein down their concentration gradient without any ATP. Only pumps use ATP directly, and movement against a gradient always needs an energy source, either ATP used by a pump or a gradient that a pump has set up.
items.random_wrong: They allow water to cross the membrane, which is otherwise impossible for the bilayer.

items.q: A potassium channel in a cell membrane is open. Which statement describes the movement of ions through it?
items.correct: Potassium ions diffuse through, down their gradient, with no ATP used.
items.misconception: Potassium ions and any other ions of similar size diffuse through the open pore.
items.why: Channels are drawn as open tubes through the bilayer, and the word 'channel' suggests an unselective passage. Students do not see how a protein could tell one small ion from another. The structure of a channel protein makes the membrane selectively permeable: the size of the pore and the charged R-groups lining it allow only a specific ion through. A potassium channel does not pass sodium ions, even though sodium ions are smaller.
items.random_wrong: Potassium ions are moved through in whichever direction the cell requires.

items.q: Root cells absorb nitrate ions from soil water in which the nitrate concentration is much lower than in the cell. When the roots are deprived of oxygen, nitrate uptake falls sharply. What explains these observations?
items.correct: Nitrate is taken up by pumps using ATP from aerobic respiration, so without oxygen the supply of ATP falls and active transport slows.
items.misconception: Nitrate is taken up by active transport in the same direction as diffusion but faster, and the lack of oxygen slows the diffusion.
items.why: The everyday sense of 'active' is 'faster' or 'more energetic', and students know energy is involved, so they picture the ATP being used to accelerate the same downhill movement. Pumps use energy from ATP to transfer specific particles across membranes and can therefore move particles against a concentration gradient, from a lower to a higher concentration. That is what distinguishes active transport, not its speed.
items.random_wrong: Nitrate is taken up by pumps using ATP already present in the cell, so removing oxygen must have affected the channel proteins instead.

items.q: Artificial vesicles were made from a pure phospholipid bilayer. Oxygen crossed the bilayer rapidly, glucose very slowly and potassium ions hardly at all. When a potassium channel protein was inserted into the bilayer, potassium crossed rapidly but permeability to sodium ions and to glucose did not change. Which conclusion is supported?
items.correct: The selectivity of the membrane came from the channel protein, while the bilayer discriminated only by size and polarity.
items.misconception: The pure bilayer was selecting substances that a cell would need, letting oxygen in and keeping out potassium.
items.why: Membranes are described as 'controlling what enters and leaves the cell', which students read as the membrane making choices. They do not separate the unselective lipid bilayer from the selective proteins in it. Facilitated diffusion and active transport allow selective permeability because each transport protein handles specific particles. Simple diffusion through the bilayer is not selective: any particle that is small and non-polar enough can cross, whether or not the cell needs it.
items.random_wrong: The channel raised permeability to potassium because it is simply a small hole, so sodium ions should have crossed as well.

items.q: Which statement about glycoproteins in the plasma membrane is correct?
items.correct: Their carbohydrate is on the extracellular side and is used in cell recognition and adhesion.
items.misconception: Their carbohydrate is on the cytoplasmic side and is respired when the cell lacks glucose.
items.why: In B1.1 carbohydrates are introduced first as energy sources and energy stores, so students attach the same role to every carbohydrate they meet. Membrane carbohydrates are short chains linked to proteins or lipids on the extracellular side. Their roles are cell adhesion and cell recognition; they are not an energy store.
items.random_wrong: Their carbohydrate projects from both faces of the membrane so that either face can be recognised.

items.q: A student draws a two-dimensional representation of the fluid mosaic model. Which feature of the drawing is correct?
items.correct: Cholesterol is drawn among the phospholipids within the bilayer, not on its surface.
items.misconception: The tails of the inner layer point into the cytoplasm, as the cytoplasm is the inside of the cell.
items.why: Students confuse 'the interior of the bilayer' with 'the interior of the cell', and forget that the cytoplasm is an aqueous solution just like the fluid outside the cell. Both the cytoplasm and the extracellular fluid are aqueous, so the hydrophilic phosphate heads face outwards on both sides of the bilayer. The hydrophobic tails of both layers meet in the middle, which is the only hydrophobic region.
items.random_wrong: The proteins are drawn at regular, equal spacings, like tiles set in a fixed pattern across the sheet.

items.q: Membrane proteins from a mouse cell and from a human cell were labelled with different coloured markers and the two cells were fused. After about 40 minutes the two colours were fully intermixed over the surface of the fused cell. What does this show?
items.correct: Proteins can move laterally through the bilayer, so the membrane is fluid and proteins are not held in a fixed pattern.
items.misconception: The membrane developed gaps as it became more fluid, allowing the labelled proteins to leak through them.
items.why: The everyday meaning of 'fluid' is a liquid that flows and can be poured, so students imagine gaps opening up in a loose liquid film. Fluidity means that the components of the membrane are free to move sideways past one another. The bilayer remains continuous, with the hydrophobic core intact, so it stays an effective barrier to ions and polar molecules.
items.random_wrong: The proteins from the two cells were covalently bonded into a single new continuous sheet during fusion.

items.q: Why does a lipid bilayer that contains a high proportion of unsaturated fatty acids remain fluid at low temperatures?
items.correct: The kinked tails cannot pack closely, so the lipids have a lower melting point.
items.misconception: The bilayer's fluidity does not depend on temperature, so its fatty acids make no difference.
items.why: Membranes are drawn as static diagrams, and the effect of temperature on the packing of hydrocarbon tails is not shown, so students have no reason to expect fluidity to vary. Like any lipid, a bilayer becomes more fluid as temperature rises and less fluid as it falls. Organisms match the fatty acid composition of their membranes to their habitat: more saturated fatty acids at high temperatures for strength, more unsaturated fatty acids at low temperatures for fluidity.
items.random_wrong: The double bonds hold neighbouring tails rigidly together, giving the bilayer a fixed structure.

items.q: In an investigation, fish of one species were kept at 5 °C or at 25 °C for several weeks. The membrane phospholipids of the fish kept at 5 °C contained a higher proportion of unsaturated fatty acids than those of the fish kept at 25 °C. What is the best explanation?
items.correct: At 5 °C membranes rich in saturated fatty acids would stiffen, so the fish increase unsaturated ones to stay fluid.
items.misconception: At 5 °C the extra unsaturated fatty acids insulate the cells against heat loss, as fat does in polar animals.
items.why: Students know that animals in cold climates have thick layers of insulating fat, and that saturated fats are solid, so they reason that cold-adapted cells should also be rich in saturated fat. Membrane fluidity is what matters, not insulation. At low temperatures a membrane rich in saturated fatty acids would stiffen, so cold-habitat organisms such as fish in polar or deep water have a higher proportion of unsaturated fatty acids, which have lower melting points and keep the membrane fluid.
items.random_wrong: At 5 °C unsaturated fatty acids are needed to make the membranes more rigid, so that they hold their shape firmly in the cold.

items.q: Which statement describes cholesterol in an animal cell membrane?
items.correct: It lies in the bilayer between phospholipids and adjusts fluidity in both directions.
items.misconception: It lies within the bilayer between phospholipids and acts solely to reduce membrane fluidity.
items.why: Cholesterol is met in health contexts as something that hardens arteries, and simplified notes say 'cholesterol reduces fluidity' without the qualification about temperature. Cholesterol acts as a modulator (adjustor) of membrane fluidity in animal cells, stabilizing membranes at higher temperatures and preventing stiffening at lower temperatures. Its effect is to keep fluidity within a working range across a range of temperatures.
items.random_wrong: It is attached to the outer surface of the bilayer and makes the membrane stiffer and stronger.

items.q: Two artificial membranes are made from the same phospholipids, one with cholesterol added and one without. Both are cooled to a temperature at which the membrane without cholesterol becomes stiff. What is expected for the membrane with cholesterol?
items.correct: It remains more fluid than the membrane without cholesterol, because cholesterol prevents the tails from packing closely.
items.misconception: It is unchanged, because cholesterol on the membrane surface cannot affect the packing of the tails inside.
items.why: In some diagrams cholesterol is drawn as a separate blob, and students who see it as an 'extra' rather than as an amphipathic lipid place it outside the bilayer. Cholesterol is mostly hydrophobic with a small hydrophilic hydroxyl group, so like a phospholipid it is positioned within the bilayer, hydroxyl group towards the surface and rings among the tails. This position is what lets it affect how closely the tails pack.
items.random_wrong: It becomes stiffer than the membrane without cholesterol, because cholesterol reduces fluidity at any temperature.

items.q: A phagocytic white blood cell engulfs a bacterium, enclosing it in a vesicle inside the cell. Which statement about this process is correct?
items.correct: It is endocytosis, which depends on the membrane being fluid enough to bend, pinch off and re-seal.
items.misconception: It is endocytosis, in which the membrane is deformed and pinched off without needing any ATP.
items.why: Students have learnt that 'active transport uses pumps and ATP' and that everything else is passive, so a process without a pump is filed under passive. Forming a vesicle from the plasma membrane and moving it, or moving a vesicle to the membrane and fusing it, require ATP. Endocytosis and exocytosis are active processes, even though they use vesicles rather than pumps.
items.specStatementText: Vesicles form and fuse because membranes are fluid (HL)
items.random_wrong: It is endocytosis, in which the bacterium is pulled in through a large channel protein into a vesicle.

items.q: At a synapse, neurotransmitter stored in vesicles is released into the synaptic cleft. How does the neurotransmitter leave the presynaptic neuron?
items.correct: The vesicle membrane fuses with the plasma membrane by exocytosis, releasing the contents outside.
items.misconception: The vesicle bursts inside the neuron and the neurotransmitter diffuses out through the lipid bilayer.
items.why: Students have just learnt that substances cross membranes through proteins, and try to fit large molecules into the same picture. 'Release' suggests bursting. Proteins are far too large to pass through channels. In exocytosis the membrane of the vesicle merges with the plasma membrane, which is only possible because both membranes are fluid, and the vesicle contents are released outside without ever crossing a bilayer.
items.specStatementText: Vesicles form and fuse because membranes are fluid (HL)
items.random_wrong: The vesicle docks at a channel protein through which the neurotransmitter is passed out of the cell.

items.q: Acetylcholine released at a synapse binds to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on the postsynaptic membrane. What happens as a result?
items.correct: The receptor's channel opens and sodium ions diffuse into the neuron down their gradient.
items.misconception: The receptor opens and the acetylcholine molecules pass through it into the postsynaptic neuron.
items.why: Students learn that a neurotransmitter 'crosses the synapse' and that the receptor is a channel, and join the two ideas so that the neurotransmitter appears to travel through the channel. The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor is a neurotransmitter-gated ion channel: binding of acetylcholine to sites on the outer face changes its shape and opens a pore through which sodium ions diffuse down their concentration gradient. Acetylcholine stays outside and is later broken down in the synaptic cleft.
items.random_wrong: The receptor uses ATP to pump sodium ions into the postsynaptic neuron, depolarizing it.

items.q: Which statement about voltage-gated sodium channels in the membrane of a neuron is correct?
items.correct: They open in response to a change in membrane potential and allow sodium ions to diffuse down their gradient.
items.misconception: They open when acetylcholine binds to them and allow sodium ions to diffuse down their gradient.
items.why: The two kinds of gated channel are introduced together and both open during synaptic transmission, so students merge them into one channel with one trigger. Neurotransmitter-gated channels such as the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor open when their specific neurotransmitter binds. Voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels open in response to a change in the membrane potential; the depolarization caused by the neurotransmitter-gated channels is what triggers them.
items.random_wrong: They open in response to a change in membrane potential and pump sodium ions in using ATP.

items.q: Which sequence correctly describes one cycle of the sodium–potassium pump?
items.correct: Three sodium ions bind inside; ATP phosphorylates the pump; they are released outside; two potassium ions bind and are released inside.
items.misconception: Three potassium ions bind inside; ATP phosphorylates the pump; they are released outside; two sodium ions then bind and are released inside.
items.why: Students memorise the pump without linking it to the gradients it creates. Because sodium ions rush into a neuron during an action potential, they assume the pump also moves sodium inwards. Sodium concentration is high outside the cell and potassium concentration is high inside because the pump moves sodium out and potassium in, against the gradients. The inward flow of sodium during an action potential is diffusion through voltage-gated channels down the gradient the pump created.
items.random_wrong: One sodium ion binds inside; ATP phosphorylates the pump; it is released outside; one potassium ion binds and is released inside.

items.q: Epithelial cells from the small intestine were treated with a substance that inhibits sodium–potassium pumps. Uptake of glucose from the lumen by the cells fell sharply, although the sodium-dependent glucose cotransporters themselves were not affected by the substance. What explains this result?
items.correct: Without the pumps, sodium accumulated in the cells, so there was no sodium gradient to drive glucose uptake.
items.misconception: The inhibitor stopped the cotransporters hydrolysing ATP, which they need to move glucose against its gradient.
items.why: Students learn 'active transport = ATP' as a rule, and do not know that a gradient of one substance can serve as a store of energy to move another. This is indirect active transport. Sodium–potassium pumps use ATP to keep the sodium concentration in the cell low; sodium ions then flow back in through the cotransporter down their gradient, and this drives glucose in against its gradient.
items.random_wrong: Glucose is normally absorbed by simple diffusion, and the inhibitor made the lipid bilayer impermeable to it.

items.q: How do cells lining the nephron reabsorb glucose from the filtrate when the glucose concentration inside the cells is already higher than in the filtrate?
items.correct: A cotransporter moves glucose in with sodium ions moving down their gradient
items.misconception: Glucose diffuses in through the lipid bilayer down its own concentration gradient
items.why: Earlier courses describe glucose as being 'absorbed by diffusion' from the small intestine, and students do not appreciate that glucose is a polar molecule that cannot cross a bilayer or that it is absorbed even when its concentration in the lumen is low. Glucose is polar and needs a transport protein. Cotransport with sodium allows the small intestine to absorb glucose even from a low concentration in the lumen, and allows the nephron to reabsorb all the glucose from the filtrate, which diffusion alone could not achieve.
items.random_wrong: A cotransporter hydrolyses ATP directly to move glucose in against its gradient

items.q: How do adjacent cells adhere to one another to form a tissue?
items.correct: Cell-adhesion molecules in each cell's membrane bind to those on the neighbouring cell, with different CAMs used for different junctions.
items.misconception: The fluid plasma membranes of the two cells fuse where they touch, so the two cells share one continuous membrane.
items.why: Students have just learnt that fluid membranes can fuse, as in exocytosis, and extend this to any two membranes in contact. Tissues are drawn with cells sharing a single boundary line. The membranes of adjacent cells stay separate. Adhesion is due to CAMs, membrane proteins that bind to matching CAMs on the neighbouring cell; the plasma membranes of cells in a tissue do not fuse with each other, and membrane fusion in this topic is between a vesicle and the plasma membrane, as in exocytosis.
items.random_wrong: A single universal cell-adhesion molecule links every cell to its neighbours in every type of tissue in the body.

items.q: A neuron is treated with a drug that inhibits sodium–potassium pumps. Over the following hours its resting membrane potential declines steadily towards zero. Why does inhibiting the pump have this effect?
items.correct: The pump normally exports three sodium ions for every two potassium ions imported, so its net export of positive charge and the ion gradients it maintains are lost.
items.misconception: The drug must also be blocking ion channels, because the pump exchanges one sodium ion for one potassium ion and so cannot affect the potential.
items.why: The word 'exchange' suggests a one-for-one swap, and the 3:2 ratio is easily dropped from a simplified description. The exchange is unequal: three positive sodium ions leave for every two positive potassium ions that enter. This net export of positive charge, together with the ion gradients it maintains, is why the pump is important in generating membrane potentials.
items.random_wrong: The pump normally moves sodium ions in and potassium ions out, so without it sodium ions no longer enter and the inside of the cell loses positive charge.

items.q: What happens to oxygen molecules once their concentration is the same on both sides of a membrane?
items.correct: They keep moving randomly and continue to cross the membrane in both directions; only the net movement has fallen to zero.
items.misconception: When the concentrations become equal, diffusion stops and the molecules stop moving across the membrane.
items.why: Diffusion is usually drawn as a single arrow from high to low concentration, and the arrow disappears at equilibrium. Students take the arrow to show the movement of the molecules rather than the net movement. Simple diffusion is the result of random movement of particles. At equal concentrations the same number of molecules cross in each direction per unit time, so there is no net movement, but individual molecules never stop moving.
items.specStatementText: Simple diffusion: no protein, no energy
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the movement of oxygen into a cell need a concentration gradient?
items.correct: Yes. Oxygen enters by simple diffusion between the phospholipids, and net movement occurs only from a higher to a lower concentration; cell respiration keeps the internal concentration low, which maintains the gradient.
items.misconception: Oxygen is drawn into a respiring cell because the cell needs it, regardless of the concentrations on the two sides of the membrane.
items.why: Students explain gas exchange teleologically ('the cell needs oxygen so it takes it in') and do not see that simple diffusion is only the outcome of random particle movement, so it happens only when there is a gradient. Oxygen crosses membranes by simple diffusion between the phospholipids. Net movement occurs only from higher to lower concentration; respiration uses up oxygen inside the cell and so keeps the internal concentration low, which is what maintains the gradient. The cell cannot pull oxygen in.
items.specStatementText: Simple diffusion: no protein, no energy
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can water cross a membrane that has no aquaporins?
items.correct: Yes, but slowly. Water molecules are small enough to pass between the phospholipids at a low rate; aquaporins greatly increase the rate at which water can cross.
items.misconception: Water can only cross a membrane through aquaporins, so a membrane with no aquaporins is completely impermeable to water.
items.why: Once aquaporins are introduced, students treat them as the sole route for water, in line with the idea that all transport goes through proteins. The role of aquaporins in increasing the rate of osmosis is misread as making osmosis possible at all. Osmosis occurs across any membrane that is permeable to water and impermeable to the solute, including a pure lipid bilayer. Aquaporins are channels that make a membrane much more permeable to water, so cells that need to move water rapidly have many of them.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why does the solute not simply move across the membrane to equalise the concentrations?
items.correct: Because the membrane is impermeable to the solute. That is why water, which can cross, moves instead.
items.misconception: During osmosis the solute moves across the membrane to even out the concentrations, and water follows it.
items.why: Students merge osmosis with diffusion and picture the solute as the thing that diffuses. The idea that the membrane is impermeable to the solute is not emphasised in earlier definitions. The explanation of osmosis depends on three ideas: random movement of water molecules, impermeability of the membrane to the solute, and a difference in solute concentration. If the solute could cross, it would diffuse and osmosis would not be needed to equalise the solutions.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a channel protein move ions into a cell where their concentration is already higher?
items.correct: No. Diffusion through a channel is passive, so when the channel is open the net movement of ions is only down their concentration gradient; when it is closed no ions pass through. Opening or closing the channel controls whether ions move, not the direction.
items.misconception: Because the protein 'helps' the ions across, facilitated diffusion can move them against a concentration gradient when the cell needs it.
items.why: The word 'facilitated' suggests assistance, and students assume the assistance includes overcoming the gradient. They also see channels opening and closing under the cell's control and infer that the cell can set the direction of movement. Opening a channel allows specific ions to diffuse through; closing it stops them. The direction is always down the concentration gradient because no energy is supplied. Moving particles against a gradient requires energy, supplied by a pump using ATP.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What happens to active transport if a cell's respiration is stopped?
items.correct: It stops soon afterwards, because pumps need a continuous supply of ATP, which cell respiration produces.
items.misconception: Active transport does not depend on cell respiration: the ATP a pump uses is already present in the cell, so pumps keep working even if respiration stops or oxygen is removed.
items.why: Students picture the ATP in a cell as a fixed stock rather than a small pool that is regenerated continuously by cell respiration, so they do not connect the ATP used by pumps to the respiration that regenerates it. Pumps use energy from ATP for every cycle of transport. ATP is regenerated by cell respiration, so poisoning respiration, removing oxygen from an aerobic cell or lowering temperature reduces the rate of active transport, while diffusion continues.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: On which side of the plasma membrane is the carbohydrate of a glycoprotein found?
items.correct: Only on the extracellular side: the carbohydrate chains project from the outer surface of the cell.
items.misconception: Glycoproteins have carbohydrate chains on both faces of the membrane, so the two surfaces of the membrane look the same.
items.why: Simplified membrane diagrams are often drawn symmetrically, and students do not learn that the two faces of a membrane differ in composition. The carbohydrate chains of glycoproteins and glycolipids are located on the extracellular side of the membrane, where they are needed for cell recognition and cell adhesion. The cytoplasmic face has no carbohydrate.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does 'mosaic' mean in the fluid mosaic model?
items.correct: The proteins are scattered irregularly among the phospholipids, like the varied pieces of a mosaic, and are free to move.
items.misconception: The proteins are fixed in a regular, repeating pattern across the membrane, like tiles cemented into a floor mosaic.
items.why: In everyday use a mosaic is a fixed pattern of tiles set in cement, so students carry over the fixedness as well as the mixture of pieces. 'Mosaic' refers only to the mixture of different proteins dispersed among the phospholipids. The pattern is irregular, and because the membrane is fluid the proteins can move laterally.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why must a membrane be fluid for endocytosis to occur?
items.correct: Because the phospholipids must be able to move and rearrange so that the membrane can bend inwards, pinch off and re-seal as a vesicle while the plasma membrane also re-seals.
items.misconception: Vesicles form by a piece of membrane breaking off, so a rigid membrane that snaps cleanly would work just as well.
items.why: Diagrams show vesicles 'pinching off' as a simple cut, so students see the process as mechanical separation rather than as rearrangement of a fluid bilayer that re-seals on both sides. A bilayer with fluid phospholipids can be reshaped and can re-form a continuous sheet after part of it buds off or fuses. A stiff membrane could not deform into a vesicle, and neither the vesicle nor the plasma membrane would re-seal.
items.specStatementText: Vesicles form and fuse because membranes are fluid (HL)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do voltage-gated sodium channels use ATP to move sodium ions into the neuron?
items.correct: No. When they open, sodium ions diffuse in down their concentration gradient; the channel is passive and uses no ATP.
items.misconception: Voltage-gated channels pump ions across the membrane using ATP, because generating an action potential needs energy.
items.why: Students know that neurons use a lot of ATP and that action potentials involve ion movement, and attribute the energy use to the channels rather than to the sodium–potassium pumps that restore the gradients afterwards. Voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels are channel proteins: they open in response to a change in membrane potential and allow facilitated diffusion of the ion down its gradient. The ATP is used by sodium–potassium pumps to maintain the gradients that the channels rely on.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the same cell-adhesion molecule used for every kind of cell–cell junction?
items.correct: No. Different forms of CAM are used for different types of cell–cell junction.
items.misconception: There is a single universal cell-adhesion molecule, so all junctions between cells are built the same way.
items.why: 'CAM' is met as one term and the syllabus does not require the individual types to be learnt, so students conclude that there is only one. CAM is a general term for a family of membrane proteins. Different forms of CAM are used for different types of cell–cell junction, which is how tissues form junctions with different properties.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025); topic B2.1 Membranes and membrane transport
